intro: Five modules follow the five Linux+ XK0-006 domains and their weights. Each has a study guide, exam tips, key terms, visual slides, and a narrated lesson. Linux+ includes performance-based questions, so pair these modules with the hands-on labs.

modules.title: System management
modules.summary: Understand the boot process, kernel modules and hardware, storage with partitions, LVM, RAID, and file systems, network configuration with NetworkManager and Netplan, shell operations, backups, and virtualization with KVM and libvirt.

slides.title: System management
script: Welcome to the system management module, the largest Linux+ domain. It's about building and running a Linux server: from boot to disks, networking, backups, and virtual machines.
Many performance-based questions come from this domain, so practice the storage commands in the labs.

slides.title: Boot and kernel modules
script: The firmware loads GRUB, GRUB loads the kernel and initramfs, and the kernel starts systemd.
Change boot arguments in etc default grub and regenerate the config. Load modules with modprobe, and rebuild the initramfs with dracut when early drivers change.

slides.title: Storage with LVM
script: LVM pools disks into volume groups, then carves out logical volumes you can grow later.
Create physical volumes, a volume group, and a logical volume, then make a file system and mount it by UUID in fstab.

slides.title: Mounts and file systems
script: Every persistent mount goes in fstab: device, mount point, type, options, dump, and fsck order. Use UUIDs so device renames don't break boot.
When writes fail but space looks free, check inodes with df dash i.

slides.title: Network configuration
script: NetworkManager profiles are changed with nmcli con mod and activated with nmcli con up. Ubuntu servers use Netplan YAML files.
Name resolution follows nsswitch.conf: usually etc hosts first, then the DNS servers in resolv.conf.

slides.title: Backups and virtualization
script: Use tar for archives, rsync for efficient copies, and dd for exact disk images.
KVM and QEMU run virtual machines, libvirt manages them with virsh, and qcow2 images support thin provisioning and snapshots.

slides.title: Review: system management
script: You've finished the system management module. Go back over the key terms and commands, and try them in the labs.
Then take the system management question set. Linux+ includes performance-based questions, so hands-on practice matters.

slides.title: Services and users
script: This module covers the day-to-day work of running services and supporting users.
You'll manage accounts and password policy, processes and schedules, packages, systemd units, and containers.

slides.title: Accounts and password aging
script: Create users with useradd, add groups with usermod dash a capital G, and lock departing users with usermod dash capital L.
chage sets password aging per user, and login.defs sets defaults for new accounts. Service accounts get a nologin shell.

slides.title: Processes and jobs
bullets: States: R S D Z T
script: ps and top show process states. D means waiting on I/O, Z means zombie.
Send signals with kill, adjust priority with renice, background jobs with bg, and schedule with cron, at, anacron, or systemd timers.

slides.title: Packages and repositories
bullets: Find which package owns a file
script: Install software from repositories, which are signed with GPG keys so you can trust their packages.
Use rpm dash q f or dnf provides on Red Hat systems, and dpkg dash capital S on Debian, to find which package provides a file.

slides.title: systemd units and timers
script: systemd manages units. Enable a service to start it at boot, and use timers instead of cron when you want logging and catch-up runs.
After editing a unit file, run daemon reload. Mask a unit to stop anything from starting it.

slides.title: Containers
script: Containers package an application with its dependencies. Build images from a Containerfile with FROM, RUN, COPY, and CMD.
Run them with ports mapped host to container and data in volumes so it survives when the container is removed.

slides.title: Review: services and user management
script: You've finished the services and user management module. Go back over the key terms and commands, and try them in the labs.
Then take the services and user management question set. Linux+ includes performance-based questions, so hands-on practice matters.

modules.title: Security
modules.summary: Harden the OS and accounts, control privilege with sudo, permissions, ACLs, and SELinux or AppArmor, authenticate with PAM, SSSD, LDAP, and Kerberos, configure firewalls, apply cryptography, and support compliance and auditing.

slides.title: Security
script: This module covers securing a Linux server: limiting privileges, authenticating users, filtering traffic, encrypting data, and proving compliance.
Expect scenario questions that ask for the most secure option that still meets the requirement.

slides.title: Least privilege
script: Give people only the commands they need with sudo rules, edited safely with visudo.
Set sensible default permissions with umask, use ACLs for exceptions, lock critical files with chattr, and let SELinux or AppArmor confine services.

slides.title: Hardening SSH
script: SSH is the front door of most servers. Disable root login and password authentication so only key holders get in.
Restrict who can connect with AllowGroups, validate the config with sshd dash t, and then restart the service.

slides.title: Authentication and logging
script: PAM decides how users authenticate: password quality, lockouts, and MFA are all PAM modules.
SSSD connects to directories like Active Directory. Logs and audit rules record what happened so you can investigate.

slides.title: Firewalls
script: firewalld groups rules into zones. Changes are runtime only unless you add dash dash permanent and reload.
Ubuntu uses ufw: default deny incoming, allow SSH, then enable. Both build on nftables.

slides.title: Cryptography and compliance
script: Encrypt disks with LUKS2, files with GPG, and connections with TLS 1.2 or 1.3. Check certificates with openssl.
Prove compliance by scanning with OpenSCAP, watching file integrity with AIDE, and patching by CVSS severity.

script: You've finished the security module. Go back over the key terms and commands, and try them in the labs.

modules.title: Automation, orchestration, and scripting

slides.title: Automation and scripting
script: This module is about doing work once and letting tools repeat it: infrastructure as code, configuration management, scripts, and version control.
Linux+ V8 also adds responsible AI use and monitoring concepts.

slides.title: Configuration management
script: Ansible connects over SSH without agents and runs YAML playbooks against hosts in an inventory. Puppet agents pull configuration from a server.
Both are idempotent: they describe the desired state and change only what's different.

slides.title: Robust Bash scripts
script: Good scripts fail loudly. set dash e u o pipefail stops on errors, unset variables, and failed pipelines.
Use tests, case statements, loops, and functions, and return meaningful exit codes so other tools can react.

slides.title: Python and Git
script: Use a virtual environment for every Python project so its packages don't break system tools.
Track scripts and playbooks in Git: branch for each change, commit with clear messages, and merge or rebase when ready.

slides.title: AI and monitoring
script: AI assistants can draft scripts, but you're responsible for reviewing and testing them, and you must never paste secrets or private data into prompts.
Monitoring turns metrics into alerts: SLIs measure, SLOs set targets, and thresholds trigger notifications.

modules.title: Troubleshooting
modules.summary: Diagnose and fix boot, storage, and service failures, network problems from DNS to MTU, security issues such as SELinux denials and permission errors, and performance bottlenecks in CPU, memory, disk, and network.

blocks.p: Troubleshooting is 22% of XK0-006: hardware, storage and OS issues; networking; security; and performance.

slides.title: Troubleshooting
script: The troubleshooting domain is about reasoning from symptoms. For each scenario, ask what changed, what the evidence shows, and which command confirms it.
This module gives you the patterns that show up again and again.

slides.title: Boot and storage problems
script: Most failed boots after a change come from fstab. Fix the line from emergency mode and test with mount dash a.
When a disk looks full, compare df and du, check inodes, and look for deleted files still held open.

slides.title: Network troubleshooting
script: Work from the bottom up: is the link up, is the address and gateway right, does DNS resolve, is the firewall open, and is the service listening on the right address?
If small packets work but big transfers stall, test the MTU.

slides.title: Security problems
script: When SELinux blocks something, read the denial and fix the label, port, or boolean. Never leave SELinux disabled.
For permission errors, check every directory on the path, group membership, and ACLs. For logins, check locks, expiry, and faillock.

slides.title: Performance
script: High load with busy CPUs points to CPU. High wa points to storage. Heavy swapping and OOM kills point to memory.
Measure with top, vmstat, iostat, and sar, and compare against a baseline so you know what normal looks like.
